transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I came because I’m spending far too much of my day checking things—papers, mostly, and little keepsakes. I’ll open the same folders and drawers, and those labeled boxes I keep things in, just to make sure everything important is still where I left it. And the thing is, I may have looked only a few minutes before, but I’ll feel I have to go back and check again.

It sounds simple when I say it, but it takes up so much time. I’ll think, “Now did I put that paper back in the right folder?” or “Is that keepsake still in that box?” and then I’m opening things again, looking through them, making sure, closing them, and then sometimes starting all over. It’s become upsetting because I know I already checked, but I don’t feel settled unless I check again.
When you’re checking these folders and boxes, do you have specific thoughts or worries that come into your mind—like a fear that something bad will happen if things aren’t in order?

Yes, there is a thought that comes with it. It’s not always, “Something terrible will happen” in a dramatic way, but it feels terrible to me, if that makes sense. I’ll get this little thought needling at me, even when part of me knows better, that maybe I threw away one of my husband’s old tax papers by mistake, or that I put a family recipe in the wrong box with the wrong things.

And then I can’t seem to just let that thought pass. I’ll tell myself, “No, you wouldn’t have done that, you just looked,” but then it comes back—what if I was careless, what if I wasn’t paying attention, what if I put it in with the greeting cards instead of the recipes, or in the tax folder instead of where it belongs. It makes me feel as though I’ve done something terribly irresponsible, even if there’s no real reason to think I have. So I go back and check, because otherwise that feeling just sits there and bothers me.

When you have those thoughts about possibly misplacing something important or making a mistake, do you feel a strong urge to do something specific—like checking, organizing, or counting—to make the anxiety go away or to prevent something bad from happening?

Yes, very much so. The urge is to check—mostly to open things back up and look again. I’ll have a folder closed and put away, and then a few minutes later I’ll feel this pull, like, “Just make sure.” So I’ll go back to the same drawer, the same folder, the same labeled box, and look through it again to be certain the important papers or little keepsakes are where I left them.

It isn’t usually counting or anything like that. It’s more this repeated checking and rechecking. I’ll straighten the papers a bit, look at the label, open the box, make sure the item is there, close it, and then somehow it still doesn’t feel finished. Even if I know I just saw it, I get this unsettled feeling, and checking is the only thing that quiets it down for a little while. Then sometimes the doubt comes back, and I start the whole thing again.

When you go back to check those folders or boxes, is it mainly to make sure nothing bad happens—like if a paper is lost or a keepsake misplaced—or is it more about feeling uncomfortable until you check again?

It’s more the uncomfortable feeling, I think—though in my mind it gets tied up with the idea that something important might not be where it belongs. I don’t picture some big disaster exactly, but I get this nagging feeling that I can’t leave alone until I look again.

So I’ll go back to the same folders, the same drawers, the same labeled boxes, even if I was just there a few minutes earlier. I’ll open them and check that the papers are still where I put them, or that a keepsake is still in its box. And once I’ve seen it, I do feel a little calmer, but not always for long. It’s like my mind won’t accept that I already checked.

I know it probably sounds repetitive, because it is repetitive, but that’s really the problem—I spend far too much of the day doing that over and over, trying to get that settled feeling.
Can you describe what goes through your mind just before you feel the need to check again? Are these thoughts intrusive or unwanted, and do they cause you distress?

Just before I check again, it’s usually this little thought that pushes its way in, like, “What if you threw away one of his old tax papers?” or “What if that recipe card got put in the wrong box?” It isn’t always a full, clear sentence, but that’s the feeling of it. And even when I know better—even when I can remember that I just looked, or that I’m generally careful—it keeps needling at me.

It does feel unwanted, yes. I’m not sitting there trying to think of these things. I’ll be doing something else, or I’ll have just put the folder away, and then the doubt comes back. And it’s upsetting because it makes me feel as if I’ve been terribly careless, like I’ve done something irresponsible with something that matters. I can tell myself, “You didn’t throw anything away, you checked it,” but it doesn’t settle properly until I go back and look again.
Do these thoughts or the need to check things ever take up so much time that you struggle to get through your day, or do they cause you significant distress that affects your daily life?

Yes, it does. More than I like to admit, honestly. It can eat up a whole afternoon before I quite realize what’s happened. I’ll think, “I’m just going to check that one folder,” and then that leads to another folder, and then a box, and then I notice something is slightly out of order, so I start straightening, and before long the day has gone.

I’ve had to cancel mentoring sessions because I got so caught up in checking and rechecking that I wasn’t ready, or I felt too unsettled to leave things as they were. And I’ve skipped book club too, which is embarrassing to say, because I do enjoy it. But if the apartment is in disarray from all the folders and papers being pulled out, I feel ashamed having anyone over or even explaining why I’m late or absent.

It’s not just a little nuisance. It really does interfere. I lose time, and then I feel embarrassed and frustrated with myself, because I know I meant to do ordinary things—see people, keep commitments—and instead I’ve spent hours trying to get that feeling of being sure.

Are these thoughts that lead you to check things something you experience even when you're not about to check, like when you're trying to relax or doing something else, and do they push into your mind even when you don’t want them to?

Yes, they do. It’s not only when I’m standing in front of the boxes or already sorting papers. I can be sitting down trying to have a quiet cup of tea, or reading, or just thinking I’ve finished with everything for the day, and then the thought comes in anyway.

It’s usually something like, “What if you threw away one of his old tax papers?” or “What if that family recipe got put in the wrong box?” And I may know perfectly well that I’m careful, and that I’ve checked before, but the thought just keeps needling at me. It doesn’t feel like a thought I chose. It pushes in, and then I get this awful feeling that I’ve done something terribly careless with something important.

I try to let it pass sometimes, I really do, but it sits there in my mind and makes me so uneasy that it’s very hard not to go and look.
Do you feel you have to perform these checking behaviors in a certain way or a specific number of times to feel reassured, even if you know it might not make sense?

It isn’t so much a number, no—not like I have to do it exactly three times or anything like that. It’s more that I have to do it until it feels… settled, I suppose. And that can mean opening the same folder again, then the drawer, then the labeled box, just to make sure the paper or keepsake is still where I left it.

I know that probably doesn’t sound logical, especially when I’ve only just checked a few minutes before. I’ll tell myself, “You already saw it there,” but then I feel pulled back to look again. Sometimes I need to see the label, then see the actual papers, maybe touch the edge of the folder or make sure the item is lying properly, and only then do I get a little reassurance. But it doesn’t always last.

That’s really why I came. I’m spending far too much of my day doing this—opening the same folders, drawers, and boxes again and again—trying to be certain the important things haven’t moved or been misplaced, even though part of me knows they haven’t.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms are consistent with obsessive thoughts related to the fear of misplacing important items or making mistakes, leading to repetitive checking behaviors aimed at reducing distress rather than preventing a specific feared event. The absence of a need to perform the behavior a specific number of times or in a ritualistic manner rules out other subtypes such as F42.0 (predominantly obsessive thoughts) or F42.1 (predominantly compulsive acts). The symptoms do not meet criteria for F42.8 or F42.9.
